title: ABOUT
text:
The purpose of ACE is to provide a transparent and reproducible audit of clinical evidence, specifically identifying observable statistical errors, internal inconsistencies, image anomalies, and potential violations of publication ethics. The identification of errors or anomalies in these reports are strictly objective. Findings are limited to pointing out clear and obvious data discrepancies, methodological errors, and potential signatures of misconduct as they appear in the published record.
Each report will contain a clear description of the errors and integrity issues found in one or more related articles. Including figures, tables, and screenshots of the audited article. Reports will have a unique identifier with the following format: \[
\overset{\textsf{year}}{\overbrace{\textsf{ACE}\vphantom{^0_0}}}\;\underset{\textsf{year}}{\underbrace{\textsf{2026}\vphantom{^0_0}}}\!\!\!\!\!\overset{\textsf{report number}}{\overbrace{\textsf{0001}\vphantom{^0_0}}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\;\text{-}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\underset{\textsf{version number}}{\underbrace{\textsf{01}\vphantom{^0_0}}}
\] The unique identifier will be used to reference other reports.
All version control will be done via Github. When new report versions are made public, the change log will be updated at the bottom of the report. All code will be available in the corresponding quarto report documents on Github. The online report viewer will contain drop downs for all code blocks in the report. The PDFs will not contain any code to ensure ease of readability.

title: ACE
text:
Audit Clinical Evidence (ACE) is an analytical platform dedicated to evaluating research integrity in the medical and clinical sciences. ACE independently reviews published papers for errors and indicators of potential fabrication or misconduct. To measure a study’s true impact, the platform accurately combines data from multiple scholarly databases to track both traditional citations and alternative social metrics. Ultimately, ACE aims to protect the credibility of the scientific record and encourage ethical best practices across global research.

The views expressed on this platform are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the United States Government or any affiliated agency

title: ACE
text:
The ACE Research Integrity Violations (ACE-RIV)
The ACE Research Integrity Violations is a classification system used to identify and categorize errors and integrity issues. It organizes existing standards from groups like Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), Council of Science Editors (CSE), International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), and The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA) into four main sections: Authorship and Publication, Statistical and Data Integrity, Publication Process Manipulation, and Ethical Oversight.
Each identified violation within the report will described clearly with evidence. For instance, if a statistical inconsistency is found, the report will detail the exact table or figure where the impossible data exists and explain why it is invalid. To provide a comprehensive overview, each report will open with an Executive Summary. This summary will feature a reference table that lists all violations in the report. Concluding the summary will be a clear, actionable recommendation, advising on the appropriate next steps, such as requesting raw data, issuing a retraction, or requesting a correction.
The list of violations are subject to change.

Section 1: Authorship and Publication
ACE 1.1: Guest, Honorary, or Gift Authorship

Standard: Authorship must be restricted to those who have made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research, avoiding inclusion based solely on a tenuous affiliation or an expectation that it will improve the chances of publication.
Source: Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Section 2.2.2; Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) Core Practice 2: Authorship and Contributorship.

ACE 1.2: Ghost Authorship

Standard: All individuals who actively participate in the research, data analysis, or manuscript drafting must be disclosed in the author byline or acknowledgments, preventing the undisclosed involvement of industry employees, medical writers, or marketing staff.
Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.2.2; COPE Core Practice 2: Authorship and Contributorship.

ACE 1.3: Authorship for Sale and Paper Mill Activity

Standard: The buying or selling of authorship positions on a scientific manuscript is explicitly prohibited. The use of commercial paper mills that organize on-demand writing of fraudulent academic manuscripts and offer co-authorship for sale represents a severe breach of research integrity.
Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.2.2; Researcher Connect; COPE & STM Paper Mills Report.

ACE 1.4: Plagiarism

Standard: The inclusion of other people’s work or ideas without providing proper credit to the original source.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines.



Section 2: Statistical and Data Integrity
ACE 2.1: Anomalies and Extreme Values

Standard: The reporting of data, statistics, or results that display extreme or unrealistic values, highly improbable distributions, or terminal digit frequencies that are inconsistent with random processes. Such anomalies suggest deviations from expected observations.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); Brookes (2024) Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons.

ACE 2.2: Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets

Standard: The presence of irreconcilable mathematical discrepancies within the reported data or summary statistics. This includes the reporting of statistical combinations (e.g., means, standard deviations, and sample sizes) that are mathematically impossible to derive from any empirical dataset, or outcomes that are fundamentally incompatible with the stated methodology.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); CSE White Paper, Section 3.4.1; Brookes (2024) Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons.

ACE 2.3: Selective Reporting, Suppressed Data, and Omitted Methodology

Standard: The selective publication of research outcomes, characterized by the unjustifiable omission or suppression of data, negative results, or conflicting findings that are relevant to the study’s conclusions. In the context of clinical research, this includes, but is not limited to, the failure to report all primary and secondary outcomes as they were originally prospectively registered in a clinical trial registry. Additionally this integrity standard includes the withholding of methodological details, experimental procedures, or analytical procedures necessary for the independent verification and reproducibility of the results.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work; Singapore Statement on Research Integrity.

ACE 2.4: Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting

Standard: The inaccurate calculation, transcription, or reporting of quantitative data and statistical results. This encompasses observable calculation errors, discrepancies between presented raw data and derived summary statistics, and the misuse of statistical methods to inappropriately suggest or alter statistical significance.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); Brookes (Misconduct Detection—Evolving Methods & Lessons); Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).



Section 3: Publication Process Manipulation
ACE 3.1: Duplicate Publication and Salami Slicing

Standard: Authors must avoid duplicate publication by not reproducing verbatim content from their own previously published work. Additionally, chopping up research results into multiple smaller papers with the specific aim of artificially increasing publication counts (“salami publications”) is an unacceptable practice.
Source: Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Section 2.2.6; The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); ICMJE Recommendations for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals, Section III.D.2; COPE Core Practice 7: Intellectual Property.

ACE 3.2: Citation Manipulation

Standard: Any systematic practice that inappropriately pressures authors to cite material with the primary goal of boosting citation rates.
Source: CSE White Paper, Section 2.1.5; The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines

ACE 3.3: Peer Review Subversion

Standard: The manipulation of the peer review process, such as participating in groups of reviewers and authors colluding to review each other’s publications, undermines the quality control of research. The exchange of payment for the allowance of fake reviewer reports is a known predatory practice.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA); United2Act Paper Mill Guidelines; Patterns of Paper Mill Papers and Retraction Challenges (Peer Review Congress); COPE Core Practice 9: Peer Review Processes



Section 4: Ethical Oversight and Transparency
ACE 4.1: Failure to Disclose Conflicts of Interest (COI)

Standard: Researchers should clearly disclose any financial and other conflicts of interest that could compromise the trustworthiness of their work in research proposals, publications, and public communications.
Source: Singapore Statement on Research Integrity, Principle 9; Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Sections 2.1.3 & 2.1.4; COPE Core Practice 4: Conflicts of Interest / Competing Interests; ICMJE Recommendations and Form for Disclosure of Potential Conflicts of Interest; Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).

ACE 4.2: Evasion of Ethical Oversight

Standard: Researchers must handle research participants and subjects with respect and care, and strictly in accordance with legal provisions and ethical principles.
Source: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA), Section 2.4; Council of Science Editors (CSE) White Paper, Sections 2.2.6 & 3.1.1; COPE Core Practice 6: Ethical Oversight; Fostering Integrity in Research (National Academies of Sciences).

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
The ACE Research Integrity Violations framework is a classification system used to identify and categorize scientific errors and integrity issues in academic publishing. It synthesizes existing standards from global authorities such as: the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the Council of Science Editors (CSE), the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), and the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA)—into four primary domains: Authorship and Publication, Statistical and Data Integrity, Ethical Oversight, and Minor Errors.
Within ACE audit reports, each identified violation is described clearly and backed by objective evidence. For instance, if a statistical inconsistency is found, the report will detail the exact table or figure containing the impossible data and explain why it is invalid. To provide a comprehensive overview, each report opens with an Executive Summary featuring a reference table of all RIVs found in the study. The summary concludes with a clear, actionable recommendation advising on appropriate next steps, such as requesting raw data, issuing a correction, or initiating a full retraction. Rather than conducting systemic reviews of the literature to identify problematic clinical research, ACE uses personal and others’ expertise, leads, and potential signatures of misconduct. Ultimately, ACE focuses its resources on producing comprehensive audit reports for papers exhibiting severe integrity violations, meaning the vast majority of these audits will conclude with a recommendation for retraction.
(Note: The following list of standard violations is subject to ongoing updates and revisions.)

title: Research Integrity Violations
text:
Section 1: Authorship and Publication

RIV 1.1: Guest, Honorary, or Gift Authorship.
Authorship is granted to individuals who have not made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research.


RIV 1.2: Ghost Authorship.
Individuals who actively participated in the research, data analysis, or manuscript drafting are absent from the author byline or acknowledgments.


RIV 1.3: Authorship for Sale and Paper Mill Activity.
Authorship positions on a scientific manuscript are bought, sold, or traded.


RIV 1.4: Plagiarism.
Another person’s work, ideas, texts, or intellectual property are included in a manuscript without providing proper attribution, credit, or citation to the original source.


RIV 1.5: Tortured Phrases and Text Spinners.
The manuscript contains bizarre, unnatural synonyms or “tortured phrases” (e.g., using “flag to clamor” instead of “signal to noise,” or “bosom malignancy” instead of “breast cancer”).


RIV 1.6: Duplicate Publication and Salami Slicing.
Content or findings from previously published work are reproduced verbatim without explicit disclosure and justification. This also encompasses “salami slicing,” where a single coherent body of research is segmented into multiple smaller papers, expanding publication counts without adding proportionate scientific value.


RIV 1.7: Citation Manipulation.
Systematic practices are employed to force or pressure the citation of specific material, resulting in artificially elevated citation metrics for an author, journal, or institution.


RIV 1.8: Peer Review Subversion.
The independent peer review process is bypassed or compromised. This includes participating in “collusion rings” (where groups of reviewers and authors coordinate to automatically approve each other’s publications) or the exchange of payment or favors for the allowance of uncritical or hijacked peer review reports.


RIV 1.9: Irrelevant Citations and Reference Padding.
Distinct from citation manipulation (ACE-RIV 1.7), this involves injecting citations into the bibliography that have absolutely no semantic relevance to the surrounding text. This is a common paper mill tactic where references are sold to researchers to artificially boost their h-index, resulting in physics papers bizarrely citing clinical oncology research.


RIV 1.10: Trial Registration and Protocol Deviations.
The manuscript reports results from a clinical trial or pre-registered study that either failed to register in a recognized public database (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov) prior to the onset of subject enrollment, or contains significant, undisclosed deviations from the original pre-registered protocol.

title: Integrity Violations
text:
The ACE Research Integrity Violations (ACE-RIV)
The ACE Research Integrity Violations framework is a classification system used to identify and categorize anomalies and integrity issues in academic publishing. It synthesizes existing standards from global authorities such as: the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the Council of Science Editors (CSE), the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), and the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (ALLEA)—into four primary domains: Authorship and Publication, Statistical and Data Integrity, Publication Process Manipulation, and Ethical Oversight.
Within ACE reports, each identified violation is described clearly and backed by objective evidence. For instance, if a statistical inconsistency is found, the report will detail the exact table or figure containing the impossible data and explain why it is invalid. To provide a comprehensive overview, each report opens with an Executive Summary featuring a reference table of all total number violations. The summary concludes with a clear, actionable recommendation advising on appropriate next steps, such as requesting raw data, issuing a correction, or initiating a full retraction.
(Note: The following list of standard violations is subject to ongoing updates and revisions.)

Section 1: Authorship and Publication

ACE 1.1: Guest, Honorary, or Gift Authorship
Authorship is granted to individuals who have not made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research. This typically occurs when individuals are included based solely on a tenuous professional affiliation or a position of authority, regardless of their actual involvement in the work.
ACE 1.2: Ghost Authorship
Individuals who actively participated in the research, data analysis, or manuscript drafting are absent from the author byline or acknowledgments. This includes the undisclosed involvement of industry employees, contracted medical writers, or marketing staff.
ACE 1.3: Authorship for Sale and Paper Mill Activity
Authorship positions on a scientific manuscript are bought, sold, or traded. This includes the use of commercial “paper mills” that generate on-demand academic manuscripts and offer co-authorship for a fee.
ACE 1.4: Plagiarism
Another person’s work, ideas, texts, or intellectual property are included in a manuscript without providing proper attribution, credit, or citation to the original source.




Section 2: Statistical and Data Integrity
ACE 2.1: Anomalies and Extreme Values Violative Condition: The reported data, statistics, or results display extreme, unrealistic values, highly improbable distributions, or terminal digit frequencies that are mathematically inconsistent with random, natural processes.
ACE 2.2: Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets Violative Condition: Irreconcilable mathematical discrepancies exist within the reported data or summary statistics. This includes reporting combinations of statistics (e.g., means, standard deviations, and sample sizes) that are mathematically impossible to derive from any empirical dataset, or outcomes that are fundamentally incompatible with the stated methodology.
ACE 2.3: Selective Reporting, Suppressed Data, and Omitted Methodology Violative Condition: Published outcomes exclude relevant data, negative results, or conflicting findings that impact the study’s conclusions. In clinical research, this includes the failure to report all primary and secondary outcomes as prospectively registered in a trial registry. This condition also applies when critical methodological or analytical details necessary for independent verification and reproducibility are absent.
ACE 2.4: Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting Violative Condition: Quantitative data and statistical results are inaccurately calculated, transcribed, or reported. This encompasses observable mathematical errors, discrepancies between presented raw data and derived summary statistics, and the misapplication of statistical methods resulting in unsupported statistical significance.



Section 3: Publication Process Manipulation
ACE 3.1: Duplicate Publication and Salami Slicing Violative Condition: Content or findings from previously published work are reproduced verbatim without explicit disclosure and justification. This also encompasses “salami slicing,” where a single coherent body of research is segmented into multiple smaller papers, expanding publication counts without adding proportionate scientific value.
ACE 3.2: Citation Manipulation Violative Condition: Systematic practices are employed to force or pressure the citation of specific material, resulting in artificially elevated citation metrics for an author, journal, or institution.
ACE 3.3: Peer Review Subversion Violative Condition: The independent peer review process is bypassed or compromised. This includes participating in “collusion rings” (where groups of reviewers and authors coordinate to automatically approve each other’s publications) or the exchange of payment or favors for the allowance of uncritical or hijacked peer review reports.



Section 4: Ethical Oversight and Transparency
ACE 4.1: Failure to Disclose Conflicts of Interest (COI) Violative Condition: Financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest are not disclosed in research proposals, publications, or public communications, where such associations could be perceived by readers or reviewers as compromising the objectivity of the work.
ACE 4.2: Bypass of Ethical Oversight Violative Condition: Required institutional ethical oversight committees (such as IRBs or animal care committees) are bypassed, or research participants (human or animal) are not handled strictly in accordance with established legal provisions, safety regulations, and ethical principles.

text:
Section 2: Statistical and Data Integrity

RIV 2.1: Anomalies and Extreme Values.
The reported data, statistics, or results display extreme, unrealistic values, or highly improbable distributions that are exceedingly unusual with random, natural processes.


RIV 2.2: Statistical Inconsistencies and Impossible Data Sets.
Statistics and data that are internally incompatible with one another (e.g., reported p value and sample size does not match reported t value). Statistics that are impossible to come from a real data set (e.g., a proportion of .83 can not possibly occur from a data set of five patients)


RIV 2.3: Selective Reporting, Suppressed Data, and Omitted Methodology.
Published outcomes exclude relevant data, negative results, or conflicting findings that impact the study’s conclusions. This violation also applies when important aspects of the study’s methodology that are necessary for independent verification and reproducibility are absent.


RIV 2.4: Data Miscalculation or Erroneous Reporting.
Quantitative data and statistical results are inaccurately calculated, transcribed, or reported.


RIV 2.5: Image and Figure Manipulation.
Images, figures, or graphical data contain duplicated, spliced, rotated, or artificially generated elements. This violation includes taking images from other websites, people, or papers and advertising it as your own. This also applies when images, figures, or graphical data from previously published works or external sources are presented as original findings without proper attribution and authorization.


RIV 2.6: Data Set Anomalies.
The raw dataset exhibits structural irregularities or improper manual alterations that compromise data integrity. Examples include unexplained duplicate records, artificially injected or unjustifiably deleted rows (data trimming), manual cell overwrites, and fundamental transcription or miscalculation errors.

Section 3: Ethical Oversight and Transparency

RIV 3.1: Failure to Disclose Conflicts of Interest (COI).
Financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest are not disclosed in research proposals, publications, or public communications, where such associations could be perceived by readers or reviewers as compromising the objectivity of the work.


RIV 3.2: Bypass of Ethical Oversight.
Required institutional ethical oversight committees (such as IRBs or animal care committees) are bypassed, or research participants (human or animal) are not handled strictly in accordance with established legal provisions, safety regulations, and ethical principles.


RIV 3.3: Ethics Approval Anomalies.
The ethics approval or IRB (Institutional Review Board) number provided in the manuscript is fake, belongs to a completely different study, or is attributed to an ethics committee that does not actually exist at the specified institution.

Section 4: Minor Errors

RIV 4.1: Minor Typographical Error.
The manuscript contains spelling errors, grammatical mistakes, formatting inconsistencies, or minor transcription typos that do not alter the underlying data, the statistical significance, or the overall scientific conclusions of the research. These errors may affect meta-analyses or secondary analyses.


RIV 4.2: Signatures of Publication Mill Work.
Several flags or characteristic patterns within the manuscript suggest the potential involvement of a paper mill. These indicators include the use of suspicious or non-institutional email domains (such as generic or disposable accounts), unusual dispersion of author affiliations across countries, authors with high number of retracted papers, authors with many publications in disparate fields, authors with unrealistically high publication rate, high rate of self-publication, and boilerplate text or formatting that closely mirrors unrelated submissions.
